catalog_quote: [p.115] 3. The phonological word. A word is characterized by the pauses which may precede and follow a string of phonemes. A pause may not be introduced within a word, however. Stress, on the other hand, is not a feature of words in the Konzime language. Phonological words may consist of one or of many syllables. ... [p.119] Syllabicity is one of the phonological "primes", rather difficult to define. In a tonal language such as Konzime, the nucleus of a syllable carries a contrastive tone and is thereby identifiable. The schewa which occurs between consonants which meet across syllable boundaries is not capable of bearing a contrastive tone ... [p.125] Of the 2.500 words I have recorded, all but approximately 46 have bitonal stems. The exceptions include 6 words having monotonal stems and approximately 40 words having tritonal stems. Since all stems are either monosyllabic or disyllabic…

new_statements.quote: There are two tonemes, /High/ and /Low/. These tonemes occur singly and in sequences. The sequences may consist of two or three tonemes per syllable peak. These sequences may consist of the same toneme or of both tonemes. Support for this interpretation is found in the tone patterns of one- and two-syllable radicals. If monosyllabic words with level tone are analysed as bearing two identical tones, then the same tone patterns are found over monosyllabic and disyllabic words. Only 39 words out of over 2,400 have a different pattern. [scanned of the scan renders 'tonemes' as 'tonet^es'/'tonetnes'; normalised here]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Koonzime has an empty rule. This source fixes the prosodic type as a two-level tone language and is silent on word stress (no statement that stress exists or is absent), so it is compatible with, and adds to, the blank record; it neither supports nor contradicts any stress placement. Scan covers body pp. 3-58 (PDF page n = book page n+2); the front matter (iii pp.) and the xxi-page appendices are not in the archive.org copy.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The work describes Koonzime (Lomie dialect) as a two-toneme language (High, Low), with tone sequences of two or three tonemes per syllable peak yielding 14 tone patterns over mono- and disyllabic radicals, plus a utterance-final lowering rule (p. 39: 'The lowering effect of the utterance-final position is counteracted if the penultimate tone is /High/') and two contrastive intonation contours (sentence-medial rise = focus; sentence-final rise = interrogative, p. 41). The words 'stress', 'accent' and 'prominence' do not occur anywhere in the 57 scanned pages; no word-level stress is posited or denied. Sections on the syllable (4), the radical (5) and the phonological word (6) treat only segmental shape, tone and affixation.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. On tone: 39 of 2,400+ words carry a third toneme (tone cluster) outside the eight basic patterns (p. 35).
new_statements.identity_note: Beavon 1977 analyses 'Konsime' = Koonzime [ozm], specifically the Lomie dialect, and in section 7 (pp. 57-58) distinguishes three subdialects of that dialect (a 'progressive' and an 'intermediate' subdialect are named; they differ in /p/ > [h] and the placement of the /si/ morpheme). Beavon 1984's record lists subject language Koonzime [ozm] with no dialect stated.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding sentence is verbatim on the Persee page scan we hold of Beavon 1983 p.115 (viewed) and in the held publisher scanned; the p.119 and p.125 supporting segments are also present. (2) The classification rests on the language's only published phonology (Beavon 1983, Africana Linguistica, 28 pp.), written by the principal describer, which states outright that stress is not a feature of Konzime words and analyses all prosody as H/L tone plus sentence intonation. Glottolog has no reference grammar for koon1245; its other 'phonology' entries are the 1977 unpublished precursor ms, a mis-tagged discourse study, and a mis-attached Gwa paper. SIL's archive (the Internet Archive listing, 39 items) adds only Beavon 1984 'Tone and intonation in Konzime' (15 pp., print-only). downloaded now: Beavon 1991 (verbal system; two-tone analysis, silent on stress, consistent) and a truncated Cheucle 2014

sources.quote: 'There is a simple two-tone distinction in Koozime, and there is also a small set of morphemes with toneless vowels.' No mention of stress or accent anywhere in pp.1-14; prosody handled entirely as H/L tone plus floating/replacive tonal morphemes. Describes Upriver Bajwe'e subdialect (1983 article describes Lomie/Nzime).
